Voiced alveolo-palatal affricate [dʑ], close front [i], moraic nasal [ɴ]; from 神 'god/spirit'

pronunciation.approximation: 'RAH-ee-jeen' — the 'r' is a light tap, and the final 'n' is a soft nasal.
pronunciation.note: Raijin is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is the thunder god, often paired with Fūjin at temple gates.

domains.title: God of Thunder and Lightning
domains.subtitle: Storms, Drums, and Temple Guardianship
domains.lead: Raijin is the thunder god of Japan, a fierce, demon-like kami who beats drums to create thunder and hurls lightning bolts. He is the brother or counterpart of Fūjin, the wind god, and the two are often depicted together at the gates of Buddhist temples, where their terrifying forms ward off evil.

cards.name: Thunder Drummer

cards.name: Lightning Hurling

mythology.lead: Raijin's mythology blends the birth-of-the-kami narratives of the Kojiki with Buddhist guardian iconography.

myths.title: Birth from Izanami's Corpse
myths.text: After Izanami died giving birth to Kagutsuchi, numerous kami were born from her corpse. The thunder kami emerged from her body, making them older than the wind kami born from Izanagi's later purification. The demonic Raijin of later art is a Buddhist-inflected form of these primordial thunder powers.

myths.title: Guardian of the Four Heavens
myths.text: In esoteric Buddhism, the thunder deity is associated with Taishakuten (Indra) and the Twelve Devas. He protects the Dharma with the sound of thunder and the flash of lightning, driving away demons and obstacles. Temples across Japan house dramatic depictions of Raijin and Fūjin.

myths.title: Thunder and the Navel
myths.text: A folk belief held that Raijin ate the navels of children during thunderstorms. Parents warned children to hide their bellies during storms, and the custom of covering the navel persists in Japan as a protection against thunder and cold.

lore.syncretism: Raijin descends from Indian Indra via Chinese Taishakuten and merges with native Japanese thunder kami. His visual form — muscular, surrounded by drums, emerging from clouds — was developed in Japanese Buddhist art and became one of the most recognizable guardian images in East Asia. The pairing with Fūjin expresses the Japanese fascination with storms as both destructive and purifying forces.
lore.culturalLegacy: Raijin remains one of Japan's most visually striking deities. He appears in temple art, festival floats, manga, anime, and video games as a symbol of overwhelming natural power. The custom of covering one's navel during a thunderstorm is a living trace of his folk mythology.
lore.extendedMeditation: Raijin is the sound of the sky's anger and the light that splits the darkness. He reminds us that nature is not merely beautiful; it is also loud, dangerous, and alive. To stand before Raijin is to feel small before the storm.

sources.name: Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (birth of thunder kami)
Bocking, A Popular Dictionary of Shinto

lore.archaeology: Raijin is best known from Japanese painting and sculpture rather than independent archaeological sites. Famous depictions include the Fūjin-Raijin screens by Tawaraya Sōtatsu and temple sculptures across Japan.
